claim: SARS-CoV-2 has infected more than 160 million people worldwide and claimed more than 3 million lives as of 2021.
source: Since its emergence in late 2019, SARS-CoV-2 has infected more than 160 million people worldwide and claimed more than 3 million lives (WHO, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to WHO, 2021

claim: Patient outcomes for SARS-CoV-2 infection range from no ascertainable symptoms to fatal respiratory failure.
source: The variance in patient outcomes is extreme, ranging from no ascertainable symptoms in some cases to fatal respiratory failure in others (Vetter et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vetter et al., 2020

claim: Comorbidities do not fully explain the wide range of COVID-19 patient outcomes.
source: This wide range of patient outcomes is due in part to comorbidities; however, prior health conditions do not explain the full range of outcomes (Zhou et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhou et al., 2020

claim: A region on chromosome 3 encompassing a cluster of chemokine receptor genes has a strong association with increased COVID-19 severity in Europeans.
source: Repeatedly, a region on chromosome 3 encompassing a cluster of chemokine receptor genes has been reported as having a strong association with an increase in COVID-19 severity in Europeans, with the strongest reported risk variant conferring an odds ratio of 1.88 for requiring hospitalization (p=2.7*10–49, COVID-19 Host Genetics Initiative, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to COVID-19 Host Genetics Initiative, 2021 with specific statistical values

claim: The strongest COVID-19 severity locus was introgressed by Neanderthals.
source: Zeberg and Pääbo, 2020 identified that the strongest COVID-19 severity locus was introgressed by Neanderthals, with a core introgressed haplotype spanning ~49 kb from chr3:45,859,651–45,909,024 (hg 19) including rs35044562, reported as one of the leading variants of the association (COVID-19 Host Genetics Initiative, 2020) and a broader, extended haplotype with reduced linkage spanning ~333 kb from chr3:45,843,315–46,177,096.
evidence: Supported by citations to Zeberg and Pääbo, 2020 and COVID-19 Host Genetics Initiative, 2020

claim: The COVID-19 severity locus was fine-mapped to two independent risk signals, one within the Neanderthal haplotype tagged by rs35044562 and rs10490770, and another led by rs2271616 just upstream.
source: Subsequently, this locus was fine-mapped to two independent risk signals, one which is confirmed to fall within the Neanderthal haplotype and tagged by a set of strongly linked SNPs including rs35044562 and rs10490770, while the other, led by rs2271616, falls just upstream (COVID-19 Host Genetics Initiative, 2021; Kousathanas et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to COVID-19 Host Genetics Initiative, 2021 and Kousathanas et al., 2022

claim: The core Neanderthal haplotype is at highest frequency in South Asian populations (30%), at appreciable frequency in Europe (8%) and the Americas (4%), and virtually absent in East Asia.
source: The core haplotype is at highest frequency in South Asian populations (30%), as well as at appreciable frequency in Europe (8%) and the Americas (4%), yet it is virtually absent in East Asia.
evidence: Specific frequency data provided for different populations

claim: The stark difference in frequency between South Asian and East Asian populations implies that the haplotype may have been positively selected in South Asian populations.
source: The stark difference in frequency between South Asian and East Asian populations implies that the haplotype may have been positively selected in South Asian populations, for which there is support (Racimo et al., 2014; Jagoda et al., 2018; Browning et al., 2018) and/or subject to purifying selection in East Asian populations.
evidence: Supported by citations to Racimo et al., 2014; Jagoda et al., 2018; Browning et al., 2018

claim: Using Sprime, 175,550 likely archaically introgressed alleles across 1,678 segments were identified in 423 Estonian genomes.
source: From this scan, we identified 175,550 likely archaically introgressed alleles across 1,678 segments (Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: Results from Sprime analysis conducted by the authors

claim: 693 segments were identified as confidently introgressed from Neanderthals using match rate criteria.
source: In total, we identified 693 such segments (Supplementary file 1c), including the segment containing the COVID-19 severity haplotype on chromosome 3 (see above).
evidence: Results from Sprime analysis with specific filtering criteria applied by the authors

claim: The U and Q95 scan identified 493 regions of introgression showing evidence of positive selection.
source: Using Africans from the 1000 genomes project as an outgroup (Auton et al., 2015), we found 493 such regions (Supplementary file 1d).
evidence: Results from U and Q95 analysis conducted by the authors

claim: The introgressed COVID-19 severity haplotype was not detected via the U and Q95 method in the Estonian population.
source: We did not detect the introgressed COVID-19 severity haplotype in our population via this method.
evidence: Negative result from U and Q95 analysis conducted by the authors

claim: The COVID-19 severity associated segment was not under positive selection in the Estonian population.
source: This suggests that the COVID-19 severity associated segment, while likely introgressed from Neanderthals based on its detection in our Sprime scan and via the work of others (Zeberg and Pääbo, 2020), was not under positive selection in the Estonian population.
evidence: Inference from negative U and Q95 result combined with citation to Zeberg and Pääbo, 2020

claim: U and Q95 scans detect the COVID-19 severity region in South Asian populations, supporting positive selection on this haplotype in South Asian but not European populations.
source: However, U and Q95 scans do detect this region in South Asian populations (Racimo et al., 2017; Jagoda et al., 2018), supporting positive selection on this haplotype in South Asian, but not European populations.
evidence: Supported by citations to Racimo et al., 2017 and Jagoda et al., 2018

claim: From the U and Q95 data, 684 cis-eQTLs were identified across 250 40 kb windows.
source: From the U and Q95 data, we identified 684 cis-eQTLs across 250 40 kb windows (Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: Results from eQTL analysis conducted by the authors

claim: No trans-eQTLs were detected in the U and Q95 dataset.
source: There were no trans-eQTLs detected in this set.
evidence: Negative result from eQTL analysis conducted by the authors

claim: From the Sprime data, 27,342 cis-eQTLs from 318 segments and four trans-eQTLs from three segments were identified.
source: From the Sprime data, we found 27,342 cis-eQTLs from 318 segments along with four trans-eQTLs from three segments (Supplementary file 1f and Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: Results from eQTL analysis conducted by the authors

claim: The introgressed region detected in the Estonian population spans ~811 kb from chr3:45,843,242–46,654,616 and encompasses 16 genes.
source: The overall introgressed region as detected in our Estonian population spans ~811 kb from chr3:45,843,242–46,654,616, encompasses 16 genes (Figure 2A), and ranks in the top 2% (ranked 21/1677) of Sprime detected segments based on likelihood of introgression and in the top 5% (58/1677) of Sprime segments based on length.
evidence: Results from Sprime analysis with reference to Figure 2A

claim: The introgressed segment ranks in the top 2% of Sprime detected segments based on likelihood of introgression and in the top 5% based on length.
source: The overall introgressed region as detected in our Estonian population spans ~811 kb from chr3:45,843,242–46,654,616, encompasses 16 genes (Figure 2A), and ranks in the top 2% (ranked 21/1677) of Sprime detected segments based on likelihood of introgression and in the top 5% (58/1677) of Sprime segments based on length.
evidence: Ranking results from Sprime analysis conducted by the authors

claim: The extreme length of the introgressed segment provides additional support that it is introgressed and not likely a product of incomplete lineage sorting.
source: Its extreme length provides additional support for the fact that it is introgressed and not likely a product of incomplete lineage sorting, which is detected as seemingly introgressed tracts of significantly shorter length (Huerta-Sánchez et al., 2014).
evidence: Inference based on segment length with citation to Huerta-Sánchez et al., 2014

claim: Four major LD blocks were identified within the introgressed segment with minimum pairwise LD of r2=0.34.
source: To examine how the introgressed segment may be affecting COVID-19 severity, we began by examining the LD structure within the segment and identified four major blocks defined as minimum pairwise LD between Sprime-identified variants within a block (min r2=0.34) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Results from LD analysis with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: All Sprime alleles in the A block are significantly (p<5*10–8) associated with increased risk for COVID-19 severity, with median p-value of 2.32 * 10–26 and median effect size of 0.42.
source: All Sprime alleles in the A block are significantly (p<5*10–8) associated with increased risk for COVID-19 severity (COVID-19 Host Genetics Initiative, 2021), with the median p-value being 2.32 * 10–26 and median effect size being 0.42 (Figure 2B).
evidence: Statistical analysis of GWAS data with citation to COVID-19 Host Genetics Initiative, 2021 and reference to Figure 2B

claim: 81.2% of alleles in the B block are significantly associated with COVID-19 severity, with median p-value of 1.94*10–9 and median effect size of 0.28.
source: The B block also harbors many alleles (81.2%) significantly associated with COVID-19 severity, with the median p-value being 1.94*10–9 and median effect size being 0.28 (Figure 2B).
evidence: Statistical analysis of GWAS data with reference to Figure 2B

claim: No alleles in the C and D blocks are significantly associated with COVID-19 severity.
source: In the C and D block, no alleles are significantly associated with COVID-19 severity, suggesting that the most likely causal variants for the COVID-19 severity association are found within the A or B blocks (Figure 2B).
evidence: Statistical analysis of GWAS data with reference to Figure 2B

claim: All 361 Sprime-identified introgressed variants act as eQTLs in whole blood.
source: All the 361 Sprime-identified introgressed variants act as eQTLs in the whole blood (Võsa et al., 2018) including for many genes that are relevant to COVID-19 infection.
evidence: eQTL analysis results with citation to Võsa et al., 2018

claim: Two trans-eQTLs (rs13063635 and rs13098911) were located on the introgressed COVID-19 severity haplotype out of four trans-eQTLs identified genome-wide in Sprime scan regions.
source: Strikingly, of the four trans-eQTLs identified genome-wide in our Sprime scan regions in Estonians, two were located on the introgressed COVID-19 severity haplotype. These two variants, rs13063635 and rs13098911, have 11 and 33 response genes, respectively (Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: Results from trans-eQTL analysis conducted by the authors

claim: 27% of response genes for rs13063635 and 39% for rs13098911 are differentially expressed in at least one experiment with lung-related cell-line or tissue infected with COVID-19 or related infections.
source: We examined whether these response genes have any relevance to COVID-19 infection and found that 3 (27%) and 13 (39%) of the response genes for rs13063635 and rs13098911, respectively, are differentially expressed in at least one experiment in which a lung related cell-line or tissue was infected with COVID-19 or other related infections (Supplementary file 1h and Supplementary file 1i).
evidence: Analysis of differential expression data conducted by the authors

claim: All 361 variants act as cis-eQTLs in whole blood, altering the expression of 14 response genes including 7 chemokine receptor genes.
source: Furthermore, all 361 variants, including the two trans-eQTLs, act as cis-eQTLs in whole blood, altering the expression of 14 response genes: CCR1, CCR2, CCR3, CCR5, CCR9, CCRL2, CXCR6, FLT1P1, LRRC2, LZTFL1, RP11-24F11.2, SACM1L, SCAP, and TMIE. Of these genes, 7 are chemokine receptor genes (CCR1, CCR2, CCR3, CCR5, CCR9, CCRL2, and CXCR6), which are likely linked to the segment's association with COVID-19 severity.
evidence: eQTL analysis results conducted by the authors

claim: CXCR6 has been identified as mediating the COVID-19 risk signal through bayesian fine-mapping, colocalization analyses, and TWAS.
source: Recent work has focused on pinpointing which of the aforementioned genes mediate(s) this risk signal, identifying CXCR6 (Schmiedel et al., 2021; Pairo-Castineira et al., 2021; Kasela et al., 2021, COVID-19 Host Genetics Initiative, 2021), CCR9 (Schmiedel et al., 2021; Kousathanas et al., 2022), SLC6A20 (Kasela et al., 2021, COVID-19 Host Genetics Initiative, 2021; Kousathanas et al., 2022), FYCO1 (Schmiedel et al., 2021), LZFL1 (Kousathanas et al., 2022), and CCR2 and CCR3 (Pairo-Castineira et al., 2021) through bayesian fine-mapping, colocalization analyses, and transcriptome-wide association (TWAS).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to recent studies

claim: Elevated CCR1 expression in neutrophils and macrophages has been detected in patients with critical COVID-19 illness.
source: The association between COVID-19 phenotypes and CCR1 and CCR5 in particular also finds support from expression studies where elevated CCR1 expression in neutrophils and macrophages has been detected in patients with critical COVID-19 illness (Chua et al., 2020), in biopsied lung tissues from COVID-19 infected patients (Supplementary file 1h and Supplementary file 1i), as well as in Calu3 cells directly infected with COVID-19 (Supplementary file 1h and Supplementary file 1i).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chua et al., 2020 and references to supplementary files

claim: Elevated CCR5 expression has been detected in macrophages of patients with critical COVID-19 illness.
source: Likewise, elevated CCR5 expression has been detected in macrophages of patients with critical COVID-19 illness (Chua et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chua et al., 2020

claim: Some ligands for CCR1 and CCR5 (CCL15, CCL2, and CCL3) show over-expression in patients with critical COVID-19 illness.
source: Notably, some ligands for CCR1 and CCR5 (CCL15, CCL2, and CCL3) also show over-expression in these patients (Chua et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chua et al., 2020

claim: The majority of alleles along the introgressed haplotype within the A block are associated with CCR1 down-regulation (average Z score = –12.3).
source: Intriguingly, when considering the effect of the cis-eQTLs for CCR1 across the entire segment, we find that the majority of alleles along the introgressed haplotype within the A block are associated with its down-regulation (average Z score = –12.3) (Figure 2C).
evidence: eQTL analysis results with reference to Figure 2C

claim: The majority of alleles within the B and C blocks are associated with CCR1 up-regulation (average Z scores = 7.1 and 10.2, respectively).
source: On the other hand, the majority of alleles within the B and C blocks are associated with CCR1 up-regulation (average Z scores = 7.1 and 10.2, respectively) (Figure 2C).
evidence: eQTL analysis results with reference to Figure 2C

claim: The majority of alleles within the A-C blocks are associated with CCR5 down-regulation.
source: When we consider CCR5 expression, it shows a more consistent pattern in which the majority of alleles within the A-C blocks are associated with its down-regulation.
evidence: eQTL analysis results conducted by the authors

claim: 613 experimental variants were tested in the MPRA after filtering for SNPs in simple repeat regions.
source: After filtering for SNPs falling within simple repeat regions (Benson, 1999), which are not compatible with MPRA (Tewhey et al., 2016), we identified a total of 613 experimental variants.
evidence: Description of MPRA experimental design with citations

claim: Of the 613 tested variants, 293 are significantly (p<5*10–8) associated with COVID-19 severity and another 15 approach significance (p<5*10–6).
source: Of these variants, 293 are significantly (p<5*10–8) associated with COVID-19 severity and another 15 approach significance (p<5*10–6), whereas 118 were not tested in the original GWAS (The COVID-19 Host Genetics Initiative Release 5) (Figure 2B).
evidence: Statistical analysis of GWAS data with reference to Figure 2B

claim: K562 cells can be induced into immune cell fates highly relevant to COVID-19 severity phenotypes including monocyte, macrophage, and neutrophils.
source: Furthermore, K562 cells can be induced into immune cell fates highly relevant to the COVID-19 severity phenotypes including monocyte, macrophage, and neutrophils (Tabilio et al., 1983; Sutherland et al., 1986; Butler and Hirano, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tabilio et al., 1983; Sutherland et al., 1986; Butler and Hirano, 2014

claim: Normalized transcript counts between MPRA replicates were highly correlated (Pearson's R>0.999 p<2.2e-16).
source: We observed that normalized transcript counts between replicates were highly correlated (Pearson's R>0.999 p=p-value<2.2e-16) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Statistical analysis of MPRA data with reference to Figure 3A

claim: Transcript counts in the cDNA samples are significantly correlated with sequence representation in the DNA plasmid pool (Pearson's R=0.24 p=2.2e-16; Spearman's ρ=0.912 p<2.2e-16).
source: As with other MPRA studies (Tewhey et al., 2016; Uebbing et al., 2021), transcript counts in the cDNA samples are significantly correlated with, but not completely explained by sequence representation in the DNA plasmid pool (correlation between means: Pearson's R=0.24 p=2.2e-16; Spearman's ρ=0.912 p-value <2.2e-16) (Figure 3B), suggesting that while some sequences do not have an effect on transcription, other do.
evidence: Statistical analysis of MPRA data with citations and reference to Figure 3B

claim: The expression of positive control sequences in this MPRA was significantly correlated with their expression in the source MPRA (Pearson's R=0.59, p=0.0058).
source: The expression of positive control sequences in this experiment was significantly correlated with their expression in the source MPRA (Pearson's R=0.59, p=0.0058) (Figure 3C).
evidence: Statistical analysis of MPRA validation data with reference to Figure 3C

claim: 95% of positive control sequences displayed activity, whereas only 14% of negative control sequences displayed activity in the MPRA.
source: Moreover, for our positive control set we observed that 95% of control sequences displayed activity, whereas only 14% of the negative control sequences displayed activity (Figure 3D).
evidence: MPRA validation results with reference to Figure 3D

claim: 327 (53%) of the 613 experimental tested variants were within sequences found to have detected effects on reporter gene expression.
source: Of the 613 experimental (1,226 alleles) tested variants, 327 (53%) were within sequences found to have detected effects on reporter gene expression (i.e., they are considered 'active' or cis-regulatory elements [CREs]) in the context of either the allele on the introgressed haplotype or via its alternative variant (Figure 3D) (Supplementary file 1j).
evidence: MPRA results with reference to Figure 3D

claim: Only 17.1% of active sequences showed a log fold change greater than 2.
source: Consistent with other MPRA studies (Tewhey et al., 2016; Ulirsch et al., 2016; Uebbing et al., 2021), most active sequences showed relatively small effects, with only 17.1% of active sequences showing a log fold change (LFC) greater than 2 (Figure 4A).
evidence: MPRA results with citations and reference to Figure 4A

claim: Active CREs are significantly enriched relative to non-active sequences for falling within K562 DNase I Hypersensitivity Sites (OR: 8.05, p=0.023).
source: We observed that active CREs are significantly enriched relative to non-active sequences for falling with K562 DNase I Hypersensitivity Sites (DHS) and within poised promoters (OR: 8.05, p=0.023) (Figure 4B).
evidence: Statistical enrichment analysis with reference to Figure 4B

claim: Active CREs are borderline significantly depleted of falling within heterochromatin (OR: 0.73, p=0.072).
source: They are also borderline significantly depleted of falling within heterochromatin (OR: 0.73, p=0.072) (Figure 4B).
evidence: Statistical enrichment analysis with reference to Figure 4B

claim: 20 expression modulating variants (emVars) were identified among the 613 variants tested using a multiple hypothesis corrected p-value less than 0.01.
source: Using this approach, we identified 20 emVars among the 613 variants we tested (Table 1, Figure 2E, Figure 3B).
evidence: MPRA results with references to Table 1, Figure 2E, and Figure 3B

claim: Only 1 emVar had an absolute log fold change greater than 2.
source: Consistent with previous MPRA studies (Tewhey et al., 2016; Ulirsch et al., 2016), the effect sizes of most emVars detected here are relatively modest, with only 1 emVar having an absolute LFC greater than 2 (Table 1, Figure 4C).
evidence: MPRA results with citations and references to Table 1 and Figure 4C

claim: Four emVars (rs35454877, rs71327024, rs71327057, and rs34041956) meet all criteria for being putatively causal variants.
source: Of the 20 emVars, we found four that meet all of these criteria (Table 1, Figure 2).
evidence: Results from prioritization analysis with references to Table 1 and Figure 2

claim: Based on eQTL and Hi-C data, rs35454877 is most likely implicated in the down-regulation of CCR5.
source: Based on the combination of eQTL and Hi-C data, the variant rs35454877 is most likely implicated in the down-regulation of CCR5, while variants rs71327024, rs71327057, and rs34041956 appear to be involved in the regulation of CCR1.
evidence: Inference from integration of eQTL and Hi-C data

claim: Variants rs71327024, rs71327057, and rs34041956 appear to be involved in the regulation of CCR1.
source: Based on the combination of eQTL and Hi-C data, the variant rs35454877 is most likely implicated in the down-regulation of CCR5, while variants rs71327024, rs71327057, and rs34041956 appear to be involved in the regulation of CCR1.
evidence: Inference from integration of eQTL and Hi-C data

claim: rs35454877 and rs71327024 fall within LD Block A, which shows the strongest GWAS associations for COVID-19 severity.
source: Of these, rs35454877 and rs71327024 fall within the LD Block A, which shows the strongest GWAS associations for COVID-19 severity and are 195 kb and 275 kb downstream of rs10490770, the most cited tag SNP for this GWAS signal (COVID-19 Host Genetics Initiative, 2021; Schmiedel et al., 2021).
evidence: Genomic location analysis with citations

claim: The four prioritized variants are significantly (p<5*10–8) associated with other phenotypes including 'Monocyte count', 'Granulocyte percentage of myeloid white cells', and 'Monocyte percentage of white cells'.
source: Furthermore, data from other GWAS studies shows that these four variants are significantly (p<5*10–8) associated with other phenotypes that could relate to the COVID-19 severity phenotype including: 'Monocyte count', 'Granulocyte percentage of myeloid white cells', and 'Monocyte percentage of white cells' (Astle et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Astle et al., 2016

claim: All four prioritized SNPs fall within ChIP-seq peaks for at least one transcription factor.
source: Finally, all four SNPs above fall within ChIP-seq peaks for at least one transcription factor (TF) (Supplementary file 1k), with rs71327024 and rs35454877 overlapping peaks for as many as 89 and 36 different TFs, respectively (ENCODE TF ChIPseq NarrowPeaks from K562, GM12878 cell lines); among others, peaks for IKZF1, a key lymphocyte regulator (Sellars et al., 2011), are found overlapping all four SNPs.
evidence: ChIP-seq data analysis with citation to Sellars et al., 2011

claim: The archaic allele at rs17713054 increases the binding affinity for CEBPB, a TF involved in Interleukin-mediated signaling.
source: On the other hand, this analysis highlighted rs17713054, a SNP belonging to the top GWAS peak, where the archaic allele increases the binding affinity for CEBPB, a TF involved in Interleukin-mediated signaling (Poli, 1998).
evidence: TF binding analysis with citation to Poli, 1998

claim: CEBPB was shown to bind the region containing rs17713054 in two lung-derived cell lines (A549, IMR-90).
source: CEBPB was also independently shown to bind this region, a well-marked regulatory element, in two lung-derived cell lines (A549,IMR-90), see Figure 2—figure supplement 2.
evidence: ChIP-seq data with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: In mock infected A549-ACE2 cells, construct pairs at emVar rs71327024 and rs35454877 exhibited statistically significant expression differences between introgressed and non-introgressed alleles, with higher levels driven by the introgressed alleles.
source: In the mock infected condition (i.e., absence of SARS-CoV-2), we found that construct pairs at emVar rs71327024 and at emVar rs35454877 exhibited statistically significant expression differences between introgressed and non-introgressed alleles in A549-ACE2 cells, with higher levels driven by the introgressed alleles (i.e., above the dashed line at 1 in Figure 5B).
evidence: Reporter assay results with reference to Figure 5B

claim: Upon SARS-CoV-2 infection, rs71327024 continued to be a significant emVar, with the introgressed allele driving 1.12 times more expression of GFP from the CCR1 promoter than the non-introgressed allele.
source: Upon infection, we found that rs71327024 continued to be a significant emVar, with the introgressed allele driving 1.12 times more expression of GFP from the CCR1 promoter than the non-introgressed allele.
evidence: Reporter assay results in infected cells

claim: For emVar rs35454877, no response was observed between alleles upon SARS-CoV-2 infection, resulting from substantial decrease in the activity of the introgressed allele upon viral infection.
source: Interestingly, for emVar rs35454877, our strongest response eQTL in the mock infected state, we now observe no response between alleles, the marked drop resulting from the substantial decrease in the activity of the introgressed allele upon viral infection.
evidence: Reporter assay results in infected cells

claim: The introgressed COVID-19 severity haplotype was not detected as under positive selection via the U and Q95 method in the Estonian population, consistent with its lower frequency (8%) in Europeans relative to South Asian populations (30%).
source: This suggests that the COVID-19 severity associated segment, while likely introgressed from Neanderthals based on its detection in our Sprime scan and via the work of others (Zeberg and Pääbo, 2020), was not under positive selection in the Estonian population. This is consistent with the previously reported lower frequency (8%) of the haplotype in Europeans relative to South Asian populations in which the haplotype is at higher frequency (30%) (Zeberg and Pääbo, 2020).
evidence: Inference from U and Q95 results combined with frequency data and citation to Zeberg and Pääbo, 2020

claim: rs10490770, rs35044562, and rs11385942, variants previously reported as tagging GWAS signals for COVID-19 severity, did not show support for expression modulation potential in the MPRA.
source: We did not find support in the MPRA for the expression modulation potential of rs10490770 (COVID-19 Host Genetics Initiative, 2021), rs35044562 (Zeberg and Pääbo, 2020), or rs11385942 (Ellinghaus et al., 2020), variants previously reported as tagging GWAS signals for COVID-19 severity.
evidence: MPRA results with citations to COVID-19 Host Genetics Initiative, 2021; Zeberg and Pääbo, 2020; Ellinghaus et al., 2020

claim: These previously reported tag variants may be likely only tagging rather than causative.
source: These variants may therefore be likely only tagging rather than causative, albeit functional experimentation in other cell lines and conditions may show otherwise.
evidence: Inference from MPRA results

claim: Two emVars (rs34041956 and rs71327024) exhibited expression modulation between introgressed and non-introgressed variants in response to SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Two emVars, emVar rs34041956 and emVar rs71327024, exhibited expression modulation between introgressed and non-introgressed variants in response to infection by the virus.
evidence: Reporter assay results in infected cells

claim: A consistent molecular symptom of severe COVID-19 response is elevated cytokine levels, particularly elevated CCR1.
source: Given that a consistent molecular symptom of severe COVID-19 response is elevated cytokine levels, particularly elevated CCR1, this variant is a prime causal variant for the association between this genetic haplotype and severe COVID-19.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of COVID-19 molecular symptoms

claim: The introgressed allele at rs35454877 drives a 1.7x increase in GFP expression with a CCR5 promoter in the non-infected state.
source: Although this allele does not show modulation during infection, the 1.7x increase in GFP expression with a CCR5 promoter that this allele drives in the non-infected state may translate to a baseline higher level of CCR5 in individuals with this allele.
evidence: Reporter assay results

claim: Upon SARS-CoV-2 infection, the enhancer with the introgressed allele at rs35454877 was severely down-regulated to the level of the non-introgressed allele.
source: Upon infection, the enhancer with the introgressed allele was severely down-regulated, to the level of the non-introgressed allele.
evidence: Reporter assay results in infected cells

claim: Individuals with the introgressed allele at rs35454877 will likely have an elevated level of the CCR5 receptor protein at least initially upon infection, which may increase their risk of a hyperactive cytokine response.
source: Although the transcriptional down-regulation occurs during infection, these individuals still will likely have an elevated level of the CCR5 receptor protein at least initially, which may increase their risk of a hyperactive cytokine response.
evidence: Inference from reporter assay results

claim: The down-regulation of the introgressed allele at rs35454877 upon infection is possibly an attempt to reduce the risk of hyperactive cytokine response, but it may not act quickly enough.
source: The down-regulation is possibly an attempt to reduce this risk, but it may not act quickly enough.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of results

claim: In the severe COVID-19 phenotype, CCR1 and CCR5 are upregulated relative to their expression levels in moderate cases of the disease.
source: For example, in the severe COVID-19 phenotype, CCR1 and CCR5 are upregulated relative to their expression levels in moderate cases of the disease (Chua et al., 2020) and we saw evidence of upreglation by introgressed alleles in our mock infection experiment as well.
evidence: Supported by citation to Chua et al., 2020 and authors' experimental results

claim: In MPRA experiments in K562 cells, the three top candidate emVars acting as regulators of CCR1 all showed down-regulation.
source: However, in our MPRA experiments in K562 cells the three top candidate emVars acting as regulators of CCR1 all showed down-regulation.
evidence: MPRA results conducted by the authors

claim: Alleles in Block A of the introgressed haplotype all act as down-regulating eQTLs for CCR1 in healthy whole blood samples.
source: Furthermore, alleles in Block A of the introgressed haplotype, which exhibit the strongest GWAS associations with COVID-19 severity, all act as down-regulating eQTLs for CCR1 in healthy whole blood samples.
evidence: eQTL analysis results

claim: The difference in direction of effect between healthy whole blood in vivo and K562 reporter assay in vitro relative to A549-ACE2 disease state reflects differential regulation of these genes in different cell types and upon infection.
source: We hypothesize that this difference between the direction of effect of the alleles in healthy whole blood in vivo and K562 reporter assay in vitro episomal condition relative to in the A549-ACE2 disease state, reflects both differential regulation of these genes in different cell types and upon infection, and possibly that these alleles contribute to the risk of severe COVID-19 by destabilizing the regulatory mechanism of CCR1 and CCR5, such that they have decreased expression in some cell types and conditions, but are hyper-expressed in others.
evidence: Hypothesis based on integration of multiple experimental results

claim: These alleles may contribute to the risk of severe COVID-19 by destabilizing the regulatory mechanism of CCR1 and CCR5, such that they have decreased expression in some cell types and conditions, but are hyper-expressed in others.
source: We hypothesize that this difference between the direction of effect of the alleles in healthy whole blood in vivo and K562 reporter assay in vitro episomal condition relative to in the A549-ACE2 disease state, reflects both differential regulation of these genes in different cell types and upon infection, and possibly that these alleles contribute to the risk of severe COVID-19 by destabilizing the regulatory mechanism of CCR1 and CCR5, such that they have decreased expression in some cell types and conditions, but are hyper-expressed in others.
evidence: Hypothesis based on integration of multiple experimental results

claim: Several genes at the chromosome 3 locus, including CCR1 and CCR5, display promising evidence for having a role in the underlying biological mechanisms of COVID-19 severity.
source: In light of the efforts of multiple groups devoted to narrowing down the genes mediating the COVID-19 severity association, we conclude that several genes at this locus on chromosome 3, including CCR1 and CCR5, display promising evidence for having a role in the underlying biological mechanisms.
evidence: Conclusion based on integration of multiple lines of evidence

claim: The involvement of most genes at this locus in the chemokine signaling pathway, and the evidence of coregulation provided by eQTL, epigenetic, and expression analyses, support the hypothesis that the COVID-19 response is modulated in a concerted way.
source: The involvement of most of them in the chemokine signaling pathway, and the evidence of coregulation provided by eQTL, epigenetic, and expression analyses, bring support to the hypothesis that the COVID-19 response is modulated in a concerted way.
evidence: Inference from integration of multiple data types
